text.p: For many Britons it is the place where their grandfathers died.

For survivors the 1914-1918 battlefields of Ypres, western Belgium, bring back memories of cramped, mud-filled trenches, of troops going over the top into soggy fields only to be mowed down by German machineguns.
This weekend will see commemorations for the 80th anniversary of the August 1917 Battle of Passchendaele, one of the most bitter battles of the First World War.
The highlight will be a ceremony on Sunday with Britain's Duke of Kent, British ambassdor David Colvin, Prince Philippe of Belgium and Belgian Justice Minister Stefaan de Clerck.

They will visit the largest British War Cemetery -- Tyne Cot -- one of 170 British and Commonwealth, French and German military graveyards at Ypres and surroundings, where almost 500,000 soldiers from both sides lie buried.

Apart from 12,000 graves Tyne Cot has a memorial to 35,000 soldiers missing after the Battle of Passendale which was intended to help Allied forces break through German lines and capture the coastal town of Ostend.

It turned into a disaster when torrential rain reduced Flanders' fields to thick mud and delayed the capture of Passchendaele, a nearby village, by two and a half months instead of the two weeks it was supposed to take.
The battle, also known as the Third Battle of Ypres, left over a quarter of a million soldiers dead and came to symbolise the futility of World War One.
Over the past week veterans, some a century old, have returned to the "killing fields" of western Flanders to honour their comrades and relive the cruelties of the war.

"I was only 17 when I joined the army, 19 when I went to France...I spent two years in the trenches, it was wicked," a 100-year-old British veteran said, speaking from his wheelchair. "It should have never happened."

While the weekend's commemorations will jog the memories of those who lost relatives, efforts have also been made to reach those -- especially younger generations -- who look to the Internet as a source of information.
St George's Memorial Church in Ypres outlines its programme for the weekend including services and a "War and Peace" stamp exhibit on the net with a link to the history of the Great War.

Canadian J. Stephens offers personal photographs, a map and a guided tour of the battle zone while an extensive military history is on offer from the Information Resource Centre at the Canadian Forces College.
But there is little that captures the war's horrors better than the poetry of Great War victim Wilfred Owen:
"If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood
Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs,
Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud
Of vile, incurable sores on innocent tongues, --
My friend, you would not tell with such high zest
To children, ardent for some desperate glory,
The old lie: Dulce et decorum est Pro patria mori"
